issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a man-made disaster trauma in a 58-year-old forensic analyst, this item is only coherent if there was a significant physical injury. The rest of the selected profile does not support an injury-based presentation: the threat items emphasize environmental danger and vigilance (limited safe places, loud sounds, unfamiliar places), while the other appraisals are about coping failure and loss of capability rather than concrete bodily injury. With no memory or strategy items to anchor a physical-injury narrative, this appraisal stands out as clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with the supplied cognitive formulation because all cross-node edges are inactive, which implies these components should not appear as tightly linked aspects of one maintaining pattern. However, the Threat items and Negative Appraisal items are strongly conceptually connected: perceiving the world as dangerous maps directly onto restricted safety zones and avoidance of unfamiliar places, creating an active Threat–Negative Appraisal linkage that contradicts the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Within the selected nodes, the content clusters into a classic mutually reinforcing danger/coping pattern rather than isolated components. 'World is a dangerous place' coheres directly with hypervigilance to sounds and avoidance of unfamiliar places, while 'Bad Coper' and 'No longer capable' reflect generalized post-trauma self-evaluation likely tied to the same threat response. With no active edges anywhere in the formulation, this degree of integration is inconsistent.

issues.item: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The formulation specifies no active edges, so the selected nodes should function as relatively isolated components rather than implying a tight linked syndrome. Here the Threat items and Negative Appraisal items form a classic connected PTSD pattern: danger-focused hypervigilance/startle and avoidance are closely mirrored by broad beliefs that the world is dangerous and that the self is incapable. This actively implies strong Threat↔Negative Appraisal linkage, which contradicts the fully disconnected formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Within Threat, the items are coherent with each other, and within Negative Appraisals the items are also coherent. The problem is cross-node/formulation consistency: the profile presents mutually reinforcing danger sensitivity and negative self/world beliefs despite all edges being inactive.

vignette: Carlos, a 58-year-old Latin American man married to his high school sweetheart, works as a forensic analyst in a bustling city. His world was turned upside down when he witnessed a devastating explosion at a chemical plant near his office. The event not only shook the foundations of nearby buildings but also rattled Carlos’s sense of security and competence. Since that fateful day, Carlos has become increasingly vigilant about potential dangers around him. He avoids going to unfamiliar places because he feels overwhelmed by the inability to assess the risks present in these environments. This avoidance extends to his daily commute; he sticks to well-known routes and refuses to visit new coffee shops or restaurants for fear of encountering unknown hazards. His body remains constantly tense, poised as if ready to react at a moment’s notice. The explosion has also left deep scars on Carlos's self-image. He now views himself as a lousy coper, believing that his reactions since the event demonstrate his inability to handle such situations effectively. This belief is reinforced every time he finds himself jumping at sudden noises or feeling jumpy in crowded places. Even mundane tasks seem daunting now; what was once second nature has become laden with anxiety. At work, Carlos’s performance has suffered due to these fears and constant vigilance. His colleagues have noticed his avoidance of new projects and unfamiliar cases, which used to be the very things that defined him as a forensic analyst. He feels no longer capable of handling the responsibilities that once came easily, leading to self-doubt and frustration. The trauma has also reshaped Carlos’s view of the world around him. He now sees it as inherently dangerous, constantly on edge and anticipating another disaster. This pervasive sense of danger exacerbates his avoidance behaviors and his tendency to startle at sudden movements or sounds. His marriage has been strained by these changes, with his wife feeling increasingly concerned about his wellbeing. What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a recent incident where he completely froze during an emergency drill at work. The simulation triggered intense panic, leaving him immobilized and shaken. This experience made Carlos realize that his fears were not only affecting his professional life but also threatening his ability to function in day-to-day situations. He is most hoping for relief from the constant tension and a return to feeling like he can handle unexpected challenges. Carlos’s current state is one of profound worry, with an overwhelming fear of losing control again in similar scenarios. His primary concern is reclaiming his sense of competence and security, both personally and professionally. He hopes that therapy will help him regain confidence in his coping abilities and reduce the constant alertness that has become a daily burden. Through this process, Carlos aims to rebuild a more balanced view of the world around him and reestablish himself as capable and resilient in the face of danger.
